article.title: How to Replace a Toilet Fill Valve
article.summary: Fix a toilet that runs, hisses or refills slowly by replacing the fill valve: drain the tank, swap the valve, set the height and adjust the water level.
article.body:
The fill valve is the tall part on the left side of the tank that refills it after a flush. When it hisses, keeps running or refills slowly, replacing it costs a few dollars and takes under an hour. Most universal fill valves fit standard two-piece toilets.

Steps

  1. Shut off the water and drain the tank

    Turn the shut-off valve behind the toilet clockwise until it stops. Flush and hold the handle down to empty the tank, then sponge out the last inch of water into a bucket.

    Done right: the tank is empty and doesn't refill.

  2. Disconnect the supply line

    Put a towel under the tank. Unscrew the supply line's nut from the bottom of the tank, where the fill valve's shank comes through. A little water will drip out.

    Done right: the supply line is off and the towel catches the drips.

  3. Remove the old fill valve

    Under the tank, unscrew the plastic locknut that holds the fill valve. Pull the refill tube off the overflow tube and lift the old valve straight out.

    Done right: the hole in the tank bottom is clean, with no old washer stuck to it.

  4. Set the new valve's height

    Adjust the new valve's height (most twist to lengthen or shorten) so its critical level mark, usually labeled CL, sits at least 1 in above the top of the overflow tube. This anti-siphon gap is required by plumbing code.

    Done right: the CL mark is at least 1 in above the overflow tube, and the top of the valve clears the tank lid.

  5. Install the new valve

    Push the valve through the hole with its rubber washer inside the tank, then hand-tighten the locknut underneath, plus a quarter turn with pliers. Clip the refill tube to the overflow tube so its end points into the tube, not down inside it. Reconnect the supply line hand-tight plus a quarter turn.

    Done right: the valve stands straight and doesn't rotate when you push on it.

  6. Turn on the water and set the level

    Open the shut-off valve slowly. Let the tank fill, then adjust the float (a clip or screw on the valve) so the water stops about 1/2 in below the top of the overflow tube, or at the waterline mark inside the tank. Flush a few times and check underneath for drips.

    Done right: the tank refills quietly, stops at the right level, and the floor under the tank stays dry.

Call a plumber if: the shut-off valve won't close or leaks, the tank is cracked, or water seeps from the bolts that hold the tank to the bowl after you've finished.

FAQ

How do I know if the fill valve is bad?

Signs include hissing, a tank that refills on its own every so often, slow refilling, or water that keeps running into the overflow tube.

Are toilet fill valves universal?

Most adjustable fill valves fit standard two-piece toilets. Some low-profile or one-piece toilets need the maker's own part.

What is the critical level on a fill valve?

A mark (CL) on the valve that must sit at least 1 in above the overflow tube, so tank water can't siphon back into your drinking water.

Where should the water level be in a toilet tank?

About 1/2 in below the top of the overflow tube, or at the waterline mark molded inside the tank.
